title: Software Developer
oneLiner: Writing the code stopped being the hard part. Knowing what to build never was.
summary: Developers built the thing that automates developers, and they did it enthusiastically, because typing was never the enjoyable part. What is collapsing is the middle of the job: boilerplate, glue code, the second implementation of something you already wrote elsewhere. What is not collapsing is deciding what should exist, holding a system in your head across years of change, and being the person who gets paged at 3am. The uncomfortable part is distributional: the job compresses from the bottom. A senior who directs three agents is more productive than ever; the junior who used to earn their seniority by writing that boilerplate has lost the ladder.

tasks.name: Boilerplate, scaffolding, CRUD
tasks.note: Nobody is paid to hand-write a REST endpoint or a settings form any more. This work is prompt-and-review.

tasks.name: Feature implementation from a clear spec
tasks.note: The model writes the first pass and increasingly the second. The developer's time moves to specifying precisely and reviewing hard.

tasks.name: Test writing & documentation
tasks.note: Generated well and cheaply. Deciding what deserves a test — and what a passing suite actually proves — does not come from the model.

tasks.name: Debugging production systems
tasks.note: Real incidents are missing context, misleading logs and unreliable reports. Someone has to form a theory about a system nobody fully documented, and be wrong in public until they are right.

tasks.name: Architecture & technical judgment
tasks.note: Choosing what not to build, which constraint to accept, and which decision the company will still be living with in five years. Models optimise the request; they do not challenge it.

tasks.name: Translating fuzzy business needs into systems
tasks.note: The requirement given is almost never the requirement meant. Extracting the real one takes arguing with people who have not decided what they want.

tasks.name: Ownership when it breaks
tasks.note: Someone signs off the deploy and answers for the outage. That signature has not moved and will not.

whatSurvives: Deciding what to build and owning what happens when it breaks — the parts that were never typing.
adaptPrompt:
You are my senior engineering pair. I direct, you produce; I own everything that ships.

Before writing any code:
1. Restate the requirement as you understand it, including what you think I have left unsaid.
2. List the assumptions you are about to make. If any of them is load-bearing and unverified, ask me instead of guessing.
3. Name the two or three approaches available, with the real trade-off between them (not a textbook list — the one that matters for this codebase).

When you write code:
- Match the conventions already in the files I gave you, even where you would do it differently. Note the disagreement in one line; do not act on it.
- Handle the error paths explicitly. Do not silently swallow anything.
- Point out every place your implementation touches something you cannot see, and tell me what to check.

After writing:
- List what you did NOT test and what could break in production that a passing test suite would not catch.
- Suggest the smallest thing I should verify by hand before merging.

Rules: never claim something works when you have not run it — say what you verified and how. If you are guessing about an API, a version, or a behaviour, say 'I am guessing' in that sentence. I would rather have an honest gap than a confident invention.
